name: Epitiostanol

lead: Epitiostanol is a DHT-derived steroid that blocks the estrogen receptor while weakly activating the androgen receptor. Bodybuilders discuss it for a drier, harder look and for limiting gynecomastia.

It has been used in Japan since 1977 as an anticancer drug for breast cancer. In premenopausal women it also suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, lowering estrogen. Orally it is broken down extensively in the gut wall and liver, so it has been given by injection; mepitiostane is its oral prodrug. No published trial has tested it for muscle or appearance.

paras: Medically it is given by injection in Japan. Physique use is based on discussion rather than documented routines.

Little safety information is published. Its prodrug mepitiostane has a high rate of virilizing effects in women. It is a prescription drug in Japan, and the related methylepitiostanol has appeared as a designer steroid.

angle.text: Epitiostanol is discussed for a drier, harder look: it blocks estrogen action, which bodybuilders associate with less water and less gynecomastia, while weakly activating androgen receptors. It has been studied in breast cancer; the appearance angle has no human data.

lead: Epitiostanol (brand name Thiodrol) is a synthetic steroid of the dihydrotestosterone (DHT) group that acts as an antiestrogen and as a comparatively weak anabolic-androgenic steroid. It was described in the literature in 1965 and has been marketed in Japan as an antineoplastic drug for breast cancer since 1977. [1]

Its interest to physique communities comes from its classification as an anabolic steroid with antiestrogen activity, and from the reported use of the drug for gynecomastia, for which Wikipedia cites Japanese studies from 1973 and 1975. [1] The appearance chain implied by its pharmacology is androgen-receptor activation plus estrogen blockade, which in other contexts is associated with a leaner, harder look. No published human study has examined it for muscle gain or other appearance outcomes. Published human work concerns hormone effects and breast cancer treatment. [2][3]
It is a prescription drug in Japan, given by intramuscular injection; its oral prodrug is mepitiostane. [1]

paras: Wikipedia reports that epitiostanol has been used in Japan to treat breast cancer since 1977 and cites studies from 1973 and 1975 on its use for gynecomastia. [1] A 1988 Japanese case report described advanced breast cancer treated with tamoxifen combined with epitiostanol. [3]

The Japanese literature describes epitiostanol as a steroidal antiestrogen, distinct in its proposed mechanism from the nonsteroidal tamoxifen. In the 1988 case report the patient had stage IV breast cancer with bone and lung metastases, relapsed four years after ovariectomy, tamoxifen and mild chemotherapy, and responded to epitiostanol; the authors suggested that when a relapse follows endocrine therapy a different form of endocrine therapy should be tried, and that epitiostanol's mechanism may differ from that of tamoxifen. [3]

Epitiostanol is an androgen receptor agonist and an estrogen receptor antagonist. Wikipedia describes it as potent as an antiestrogen and weak as an anabolic steroid, with about eleven times the anabolic activity of methyltestosterone and roughly equal androgenic activity. In premenopausal women it also acts as an antigonadotropin, suppressing the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. [1] A 1975 Japanese study examined its effects on this axis in humans. [2]

In breast cancer, Wikipedia describes the action as multimodal, with tumor growth suppressed through androgen receptor activation and estrogen receptor inhibition. [1] The page says the drug is unusual among anabolic steroids as an estrogen receptor antagonist, a statement flagged there as needing a citation. [1]

In rats given epitiostanol orally, radioactivity was absorbed but no unchanged drug was found in plasma, because of extensive first-pass metabolism in the intestinal mucosa and liver. [4] This is why the drug is injected and why the oral prodrug mepitiostane was developed. [1][5]

The oral prodrug mepitiostane carries a methoxycyclopentyl ether at position 17. In cannulated rats, after jejunal administration 7.9 percent of the epitiostanol dose was recovered unchanged in mesenteric blood and 0.03 percent in lymph, whereas the lipophilic prodrug partitions preferentially into lymph, where it travels with chylomicron and VLDL lipids. [6][7] A factors study found that epitiostanol, unlike mepitiostane, transfers from lymph to plasma. [7]

Epitiostanol is 2α,3α-epithio-5α-androstan-17β-ol, with the formula C19H30OS. Derivatives include mepitiostane and methylepitiostanol, an orally active 17α-methyl variant that has appeared as a designer steroid. [1]

Wikipedia gives no side-effect profile for epitiostanol itself. It reports that mepitiostane has a high rate of virilizing effects in women, including acne, hirsutism and voice changes, citing a 1978 study, and links to the general anabolic steroid adverse effects article. [1]

A zebrafish chemical screen reported in 2016 identified epitiostanol, progesterone and mifepristone as small molecules that lowered ferroportin protein levels, linked to progesterone receptor membrane component-1 and hepcidin regulation. This was laboratory work on iron homeostasis, not a study of appearance. [8] Animal studies in mouse and rat mammary tumor models have also examined mepitiostane and estrogen depletion. [9]

Epitiostanol is the international nonproprietary name and the Japanese Accepted Name, and Thiodrol is the brand. [1] Mepitiostane is listed as prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency, and a 2015 Japanese method used liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry to detect its urinary metabolites, epitiostanol sulfoxide and epitiostanol, for sports drug testing; the authors note epitiostanol and its sulfoxide are heat-labile and break down under gas chromatography. [5] Methylepitiostanol, a 17-methyl variant, has surfaced as a designer steroid. [1]
No studies found for muscle or appearance outcomes. Published human reports concern breast cancer and hormone effects.

A 1975 Japanese study examined effects of epitiostanol on the hypothalamo-pituitary-gonadal axis in humans. [2] A 1988 case report described advanced breast cancer treated with tamoxifen and epitiostanol. [3] Wikipedia cites Japanese studies from 1973 and 1975 for gynecomastia. [1] Related laboratory work includes rat pharmacokinetics [4], a 1977 mouse study of mepitiostane and fluoxymesterone against a pregnancy-dependent mammary tumor [9], and rat mammary cancer cell studies under estrogen-depleted conditions. [10]
